definition.text: Seventeen global goals that all UN members adopted in 2015 as part of the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development.

facts.text: The 17 goals come with 169 measurable targets and link the environmental, social and economic sides of sustainable development.
The SDGs are universal, time-bound and legally non-binding policy objectives agreed by governments.
Each goal typically has eight to 12 targets, and each target has one to four indicators, averaging 1.5 indicators per target.
Three goals focus on the environment: SDG 13 (climate), SDG 14 (oceans) and SDG 15 (land), but there is no overarching planetary goal.
On 25 September 2015 the 193 countries of the UN General Assembly adopted the agenda titled 'Transforming our world: the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development'.
The SDGs succeeded the Millennium Development Goals, which ended in 2015; critics note there are many more goals than the eight MDGs.
A 2024 UN report found only 17% of SDG targets on track; the 2025 report said 35% were on track or making moderate progress and 18% were in reverse.
Rising inequality, climate change and biodiversity loss threaten progress, and the COVID-19 pandemic slowed it.

definition.text: Indicators are the measures decision-makers use to track progress towards each SDG target.

facts.text: Targets are either outcome targets, numbered (6.1), or means-of-implementation targets, lettered (6.a).
For each indicator an expert group tried to name a custodian agency responsible for methods, data collection and reporting.
Critics worry about the large number of indicators and the cost of monitoring them, estimated in the billions of dollars.
The UN High-level Political Forum on Sustainable Development monitors the SDGs, and countries can file voluntary national reviews of their progress.

title: Trade-offs among the SDGs

definition.text: The concern that pursuing some SDGs can work against others, so that not all 17 can be reached together.

facts.text: Cited examples: reconciling ending hunger, economic growth and income equality with environmental sustainability.
Critics say the SDGs rely on dubious claims about decoupling and resource efficiency instead of addressing the tension between growth and sustainability.
Synergies also exist: the IPCC sees robust synergies between climate action and the goals on health, clean energy, cities, consumption and oceans.
Countries tend to prioritize socioeconomic goals over environmental ones, and SDGs 1 and 8 were found to be most widely prioritized.

contested_note: Scholars disagree whether the goals are internally coherent or contain inherently conflicting targets.

title: SDGs weak on environmental sustainability
article: Sustainable Development Goals#Weak on environmental sustainability

definition.text: The criticism that the SDGs treat economic growth as foundational and do not make protecting the Earth system an end in itself.

facts.text: Environmental constraints and planetary boundaries are underrepresented, and the SDGs do not pursue planetary integrity as such.
Even within the environment-focused goals, most indicators measure social or economic outcomes.
Some studies argue that planetary integrity and justice would require limits to economic growth.
A 2022 meta-analysis of over 3,000 articles found the SDGs have had only limited transformative political impact.

contested_note: Environmentalists call for redefining sustainable development in the SDGs, against their growth-centred design.

definition.text: Estimates of how much money reaching the SDGs would take, and where it might come from.

facts.text: In 2014 UNCTAD estimated the cost of reaching the goals at US$2.5 trillion per year.
A 2020 estimate put the financing gap in developing countries at US$2.5 trillion per year before COVID-19, projected to rise to US$4.2 trillion in 2020.
The 2015 Addis Ababa Action Agenda is one UN process for financing the SDGs, and private investment is seen as essential.
Blended finance is designed to support progress towards the SDGs.

definition.text: A multilateral treaty, known informally as the Biodiversity Convention, for conserving the variety of life on Earth.

facts.text: It has three main goals: conserving biodiversity, using its components sustainably, and sharing fairly the benefits from genetic resources.
It opened for signature at the Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro on 5 June 1992 and entered into force on 29 December 1993.
As of 2016 it had 196 Parties; the United States is the only UN member state that has not ratified it, citing sovereignty and economic interests.
It has two supplementary agreements, the Cartagena Protocol on biosafety and the Nagoya Protocol on benefit-sharing.
Its regulated issues include access to genetic resources and traditional knowledge, with prior informed consent of the providing party.
The idea was conceived at a UNEP expert working group in November 1988; its Secretariat in Montreal operates under UNEP.
Its Strategic Plan for Biodiversity 2011–2020 contained the Aichi Biodiversity Targets, later followed by the post-2020 Global Biodiversity Framework.

title: CBD Conference of the Parties
article: Convention on Biological Diversity#Conference of the Parties (COP)

definition.text: The governing body of the Biodiversity Convention, made up of all governments that have ratified it.

facts.text: It reviews progress, sets priorities and work plans, and can amend the Convention and create expert advisory bodies.
COP met yearly for three years after 1994 and then every two years; COP 1 was in Nassau, Bahamas.
A scientific expert committee, the SBSTTA, advises the COP on scientific and technical issues.
COP 15, planned for Kunming in 2020, was postponed by the COVID-19 pandemic and split into two sessions.

title: Aichi Biodiversity Targets
article: Convention on Biological Diversity#Strategic Plan for Biodiversity 2011–2020

definition.text: Twenty international targets for 2011–2020, set under the Biodiversity Convention, to protect biodiversity, species and sustainable use of resources.

facts.text: They were part of the Strategic Plan for Biodiversity 2011–2020, agreed at COP 10 in Nagoya in October 2010, and addressed five strategic goals.
Goal A sought to tackle the underlying causes of biodiversity loss by mainstreaming biodiversity across government and society.
Other goals aimed to cut direct pressures, safeguard ecosystems, species and genetic diversity, and enhance benefits from ecosystem services.
Countries failed to meet them because they lacked clarity, were hard to measure, went unreported and had limited funding.
The CBD mapped synergies between the 17 SDGs and the 20 Aichi targets.

title: Ecologically or Biologically Significant Marine Areas
article: Convention on Biological Diversity#Marine and coastal biodiversity

definition.text: Ocean areas identified under the Biodiversity Convention, using scientific criteria, as especially important for marine life.

facts.text: Expert workshops from 2018 to 2022 explored options for revising EBSA descriptions and describing new areas.
The aim is an international legally binding instrument under UNCLOS for biodiversity beyond national jurisdiction, the High Seas Treaty.

title: Criticism of the Biodiversity Convention

definition.text: Arguments that the Biodiversity Convention has been weakly enforced and unfair to biodiversity-rich poorer countries.

facts.text: Brazil argued that wealthier countries benefit from access to resources but give too little financial and technological support for conservation.
The CBD is described as a hard treaty gone soft, and countries face no penalties for ignoring it.
National strategies in practice neglect groups such as fungi, bacteria and protists.
Some scientists fear the Nagoya Protocol hampers disease prevention and conservation research.

contested_note: Developing countries and critics dispute whether richer nations have met their obligations under the Convention.
